source_headline: SF landlord skirts rent control laws, doubling family's rent and pushing them out
angle_statement: The exemption that let one owner double a family's rent was written to protect retirees with a single rental, and it does not count how many properties you own.
tldr: A new owner raised the Waldmans' Outer Richmond rent from $3,695 to $7,000. Their building went up in 1996, which puts it outside San Francisco's 1979 rent control ordinance.
editor_note: The exemption that let one owner double a family's rent was written to protect retirees with a single rental, and it does not count how many properties you own. California's 2019 Tenant Protection Act caps increases in older buildings, then exempts condos and single-family homes, then applies its corporate-landlord rule only to LLCs with a corporate member. Buy all ten condos in a building through a single-owner LLC and none of it reaches you. That is what happened in the Outer Richmond. Read this next to today's other housing item and the shape is clear: the protections are real, the categories they turn on are not, and rents are up 28 percent in a year while both holes stay open.
what_to_watch: Whether any state legislator moves to close the single-owner LLC exemption, which has been in the Tenant Protection Act since 2019.

fail_reasons: check_1_recap: in this story the statutory mechanism IS the news, and the note walks through the whole chain (1979 ordinance covers pre-1979 buildings, the 2019 Act exempts condos, the corporate-landlord rule reaches only LLCs with a corporate member, single-owner LLC defeats all three) plus the rent figures and the 28 percent context. A reader who reads only the note has the entire ABC7 piece. Suggested fix: state that the exemption was written for mom-and-pop landlords and does not cap how many properties one person owns, then stop. Let the reader click for how the three statutes interact.
